etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English provincial, from Old French provincial, from Latin prōvinciālis (“of a province”), equivalent to province +‎ -ial.

definitions.definition: Of or pertaining to a province.
Exhibiting the ways or manners of a province; characteristic of the inhabitants of a province.

quote.citation: 1856 December, [Thomas Babington] Macaulay, “Samuel Johnson”, in T[homas] F[lower] E[llis], editor, The Miscellaneous Writings and Speeches of Lord Macaulay, new edition, London: Longman, Green, Reader, & Dyer, published 1871, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  fond of exhibiting provincial airs and graces.

definitions.definition: Not cosmopolitan; backwoodsy, hick, yokelish, countrified; not polished; rude

quote.citation: 2011, KD McCrite, In Front of God and Everybody:
quote.text: That awful little Cedar Whatever is no thriving megalopolis, and you people are so provincial, it's appalling.

definitions.definition: Of or pertaining to an ecclesiastical province, or to the jurisdiction of an archbishop; not ecumenical.
A person belonging to a province; one who is provincial.
(Roman Catholicism) A monastic superior, who, under the general of his order, has the direction of all the religious houses of the same fraternity in a given district, called a province of the order.

quote.citation: 2009, Diarmaid MacCulloch, A History of Christianity, Penguin, published 2010, page 700:
quote.text: The Franciscan provincial Diego de Landa set up a local Inquisition which unleashed a campaign of interrogation and torture on the Indio population.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A constitution issued by the head of an ecclesiastical province.

quote.citation: c. 1503–1512, John Skelton, Ware the Hauke; republished in John Scattergood, editor, John Skelton: The Complete English Poems, 1983, →OCLC, page 65, lines 130–135:
quote.text: Or els is thys Goddis law,Decrees or decretals,Or holy sinodals,Or els provincyals,Thus within the walsOf holy church to deale  […]?
